recency_window: soft 6-month (180 days), one structural anchor permitted in the 6-12m band

sources.title: International Migration Outlook 2025
sources.date_evidence: OECD International Migration Outlook 2025, 49th Edition, published November 2025 (PDF path /content/dam/oecd/en/publications/reports/2025/11/international-migration-outlook-2025).
sources.key_claim: Permanent migration to OECD countries fell 4% to 6.2 million in 2024; labour migration fell 21% but stayed 32% above 2019 levels; labour migration policy is increasingly tailored to talent attraction with skills thresholds usually raised.
signals_supported: Permanent and labour migration easing off post-pandemic peak

sources.title: New data show intensifying unauthorized immigration decline, with large local variations
sources.date_evidence: Daniel Wilson and Xiaoqing Zhou. January 13, 2026. U.S. net unauthorized immigration has rapidly declined, turning negative in February 2025.
sources.key_claim: US net unauthorized immigration turned negative in early 2025 and averaged about -48,000 monthly through July; employment of unauthorized immigrants has contracted an average 26,000 per month, an annual-equivalent decline of about 310,000 workers.
signals_supported: US net migration turns negative as a labour-supply shock
sources.verbatim_quote: employment of unauthorized immigrants has contracted an average 26,000 per month through July 2025, or an annual equivalent decline of 310,000 people

sources.title: Macroeconomic implications of immigration flows in 2025 and 2026: January 2026 update
sources.date_evidence: Macroeconomic Implications of Immigration Flows in 2025 and 2026: January 2026 Update. Net migration is likely to be very low or negative in 2026 as well.
sources.key_claim: Net international migration dropped from 2.7 million in mid-2024 to about 1.3 million by mid-2025 and is likely very low or negative in 2026, dampening labour-force, consumer-spending and GDP growth; sustainable monthly job growth could turn negative in 2026.
signals_supported: US net migration turns negative as a labour-supply shock

sources.title: Net migration continues to fall (ONS National Statistical blog)
sources.date_evidence: Sarah Crofts, May 21, 2026. In the year ending December 2025, overall net migration stood at 171,000, down from 331,000 a year earlier.
sources.key_claim: UK net migration fell to 171,000 in the year ending December 2025 from 331,000 a year earlier, the level last seen in early 2021, driven by falling work and student visa grants.
sources.verbatim_quote: overall net migration stood at 171,000 - down from 331,000 a year earlier

sources.title: Commission reports on progress in implementing the Pact on Migration and Asylum
sources.date_evidence: Publication date: 8 May 2026. Member States have significantly advanced in implementing the Pact, which enters into application on 12 June 2026.
sources.key_claim: The EU Pact on Migration and Asylum (10 laws) enters into application on 12 June 2026 with mandatory screening and border procedures; it does not address general labour shortages, which the Skills and Talent Mobility Package and EU Talent Pool handle separately.

sources.title: 21,8 Millionen Menschen in Deutschland mit Einwanderungsgeschichte im Jahr 2025
sources.date_evidence: Pressemitteilung Nr. 128 vom 13. April 2026. 2025 lebten rund 21,8 Millionen Menschen mit Einwanderungsgeschichte in Deutschland.
sources.key_claim: In 2025 Germany counted 21.8 million people with an immigration history (26.3% of private-household population); immigration rose by only 281,000 (+1.7%), markedly slower than prior years, while employment of foreign nationals rose about 200,000 even as total employment fell.

sources.title: Population Aging and Pension Reforms in China (IMF Working Paper 2026/027)
sources.date_evidence: meta-Date: 2026-02-20; meta-parsely-pub-date: 2026-02-20. Population aging alone can slow annual GDP growth by about 2 percentage points between 2024 and 2050.
sources.key_claim: China's population aging could slow annual GDP growth by about 2 percentage points between 2024 and 2050; the 2024 retirement-age reform raises GDP growth 0.2pp annually and cuts projected pension spending from 15.3% to 11.9% of GDP by 2050.
signals_supported: Working-age contraction and ageing reshape labour supply

sources.publisher: Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis
sources.title: Declining Fertility Rates across the World (On the Economy)
sources.date_evidence: Authored by B. Ravikumar and Guillaume Vandenbroucke for St. Louis Fed On the Economy, June 9, 2026. The total fertility rate has been declining in both rich and poor countries for 60 years.
sources.key_claim: The total fertility rate has fallen in both rich and poor countries for 60 years, narrowing the gap between the poorest and richest countries from three children per woman to less than one; lower population growth is a global phenomenon.

sources.title: The Great Mismatch: How a Shrinking Workforce, AI, and Labor Reallocation Will Define the Next 15 Years
sources.date_evidence: meta-article:published_time: 2026-05-14T17:59:51+00:00. A shrinking workforce, AI and labor reallocation will define the next 15 years.
sources.key_claim: A shrinking native-born workforce, AI adoption and labour reallocation will jointly define the next 15 years of labour markets, with AI shifting rather than eliminating work and unable to fully offset the demographic gap.
signals_supported: AI and automation as a partial demographic offset

sources.title: A Shifting Pipeline: What Indeed's Data Reveals About Immigrants' Role in the US Labor Force
sources.date_evidence: meta-article:published_time: 2026-05-21T11:00:00+00:00. What Indeed's data reveals about immigrants' role in the US labor force.
sources.key_claim: Immigrants have supplied a growing share of US labour-force growth, so the sharp 2025-26 slowdown in inflows removes a structural source of labour supply that native-born workers and AI are unlikely to fully replace.
signals_supported: US net migration turns negative as a labour-supply shock

sources.title: New Jobs Creation in the AI Age (Staff Discussion Note SDN/2026/001)
sources.date_evidence: IMF Staff Discussion Note SDN/2026/001, January 2026. Authorized for distribution by Pierre-Olivier Gourinchas. (c) 2026 International Monetary Fund.
sources.key_claim: The IMF projects AI will reshape rather than simply destroy jobs, creating new roles even as it automates tasks, with the net effect on employment depending on complementarity and reallocation.
signals_supported: AI and automation as a partial demographic offset

sources.title: Building resilient societies starts with strengthening the care economy
sources.date_evidence: meta-article:published_time: 2026-04-20T08:32:32+0000. Health and education workers make up the largest part of the care economy and represent 6.5 per cent of total global employment.
sources.key_claim: Health and education workers represent 6.5% of total global employment; demographic shifts and ageing are driving up demand for care while underinvestment and a shortage of trained care workers constrain supply.
signals_supported: Care and health workforce shortage deepens

sources.title: Health workforce (topic overview)
sources.date_evidence: Evergreen WHO topic page; projected global shortage of about 10 million health workers by 2030, concentrated in low- and middle-income countries.
sources.key_claim: WHO projects a global shortage of roughly 10 million health workers by 2030, concentrated in low- and lower-middle-income countries.
signals_supported: Care and health workforce shortage deepens

sources.title: EU Talent Pool Regulation adopted to match third-country workers to shortage occupations
sources.date_evidence: On 10 March 2026, the European Parliament adopted the EU Talent Pool Regulation, an EU-wide digital platform to match employers with jobseekers from third countries in shortage occupations.
sources.key_claim: On 10 March 2026 the European Parliament adopted the EU Talent Pool Regulation, a voluntary EU-wide platform matching employers to non-EU jobseekers in shortage occupations including healthcare, construction, ICT and hospitality, targeted for completion by 2027.

sources.title: Remittance Tax Arrival Raises Questions and Action Plans
sources.date_evidence: Remittance Tax Arrival Raises Questions and Action Plans, Tax Notes, 2026/01/15. A 1% US excise tax on cash-funded cross-border remittances took effect on 1 January 2026.
sources.key_claim: A 1% US federal excise tax on cash-funded cross-border remittances took effect on 1 January 2026, applying to roughly 49 million green-card, visa and unauthorised senders and projected to cut formal remittance flows by about 1.6%, with the heaviest GNI impacts on Central American and Caribbean economies.
signals_supported: US net migration turns negative as a labour-supply shock
